full_query: A 45-year-old man presents to a physician due to difficulty swallowing and slurred speech. For the past 3 months, the patient has been coughing when he drinks liquids. His speech also sounds different according to his wife. The patient has no significant medical history. His temperature is 98.6°F (37.0°C), blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg, pulse is 60/min, and respirations are 12/min. On physical exam, he is unable to fully extend his tongue, and there are fasciculations on his tongue. When tapping the mandible at the chin while the mouth is held open, there is pronounced upward movement of the lower jaw. Sensory exam reveals no deficits. Which of the following therapies is most likely to improve survival for this patient's disease process? (A) Baclofen (B) Dextromethorphan and quinidine (C) Edaravone (D) Riluzole (E) Tizanidine

sentences: To determine the most appropriate therapy to improve survival for this patient's disease process, we need to analyze the clinical presentation and identify the underlying condition
Difficulty swallowing (dysphagia)
Slurred speech (dysarthria)
Coughing when drinking liquids
Inability to fully extend the tongue
Fasciculations on the tongue
Pronounced upward movement of the lower jaw when tapping the mandible (jaw jerk reflex)
No sensory deficits
Dysphagia and dysarthria are common symptoms of neurological disorders affecting the cranial nerves or the brainstem
Tongue fasciculations and difficulty with tongue movements suggest involvement of the lower motor neurons (LMNs)
Pronounced jaw jerk reflex indicates upper motor neuron (UMN) involvement
The combination of UMN and LMN signs is characteristic of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
ALS is a neurodegenerative disorder that affects both UMNs and LMNs, leading to muscle weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations, along with exaggerated reflexes
The absence of sensory deficits supports the diagnosis of ALS, as this condition typically spares sensory neurons
Baclofen: This is used primarily for muscle spasticity and may provide symptomatic relief but does not improve survival in ALS
Dextromethorphan and Quinidine: This combination is used to treat pseudobulbar affect, which is a symptom management strategy; it does not improve survival in ALS
Edaravone: This drug has been shown to slow the progression of ALS in specific patient populations and may modestly improve survival
Riluzole: This medication is the standard treatment for ALS and has been shown to extend survival by a few months in patients with ALS
Tizanidine: This is another antispastic agent used for muscle spasticity and does not improve survival in ALS
Given the diagnosis of ALS based on the patient’s symptoms and clinical findings, the therapy most likely to improve survival is Riluzole
Riluzole has been demonstrated to extend survival in patients with ALS
(D) Riluzole
